p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for more than a year, and the countdown clock says 366.
In Pueblo he settled Aldergrove's claim on the program's own work orders, and Nell Garrity told him why she won't ship a valve she doesn't trust: the Petrel ruined her company and her father.

The station's six spare oxygen stacks turned out to have gone into the plant in 2060 while the official list still counted them, so six new stacks will fly on Halcyon, and the agency's margin model is in question.
AR 2207 is still open, the second test article is past six thousand clean cold cycles without showing its flaw, and Ada now numbers her logs. Her margin is down to 602 days.
Then, the night the countdown hit 366, Hana asked Sam to come out to the stand alone, because she had something to tell him.
Arlo Dunn. The stand's night technician, thirty one, from Limon.
Wendell Price. Test conductor, now seventy, and the only person who can read the valve by ear.
Frances Odum. Chair of Families of Ares.
Quinn Abernathy. The scheduler, fast becoming Sam's right hand.
New in this chapter: Corinne Mathers.

Friday, February 17, 2062. 6:55 PM. The access road to the stand was two miles of gravel with a cattle guard at each end, and Sam's headlights picked up three pairs of pronghorn eyes in the ditch and then lost them. The wind was out of the north and the truck leaned into it. Hana's car was already at the bottom of Stand 2 with its engine off and nobody in it.

She was up on the deck, behind the oxidizer tank, where she went when she had something to say out of the wind. Hood up, her hands pulled up into her sleeves. The stand lights threw both their shadows three ways at once. Down on the prairie the only other building was the blockhouse, and it was dark.

Thanks for coming out. She had a sheet of paper folded in quarters, and she held it flat against the tank so the wind couldn't take it. I want to say it all the way through. If you stop me I won't start again.
He nodded and put his back against the rail.

I told you I believed it was noise. That's true. I've said it so many times it's worn smooth. What I didn't tell you is what I did with it. She unfolded the paper. It was a printed email, from her to Bea, sent Thursday, September 18, 2059, at 11:52 PM. I wrote the recommendation at my kitchen table. Downgrade to crit 2, close UNR, pick up the third attempt after the review. I sent it just before midnight so it would be the first thing she read. I'd already decided, and I wrote it up to make the case.

And in the room the next morning, when the deputy asked whether the date would move if it stayed open, everybody looked at me, because it was my valve. If anybody's told you somebody said can we, that was me. I said, can we close it now and run Wendell's attempt after the review? I made it a question so it would sound like engineering. Nobody said no. Bea signed it. Wendell found out his stand time was gone from the work order.
The wind came over the deck and pushed at both of them, and she waited for it.

Garrett wanted September clean. Everybody did. I'm not going to stand up here and tell you whose fault the room was, because I don't know, and because it doesn't matter to this. I'm the propulsion lead. Saying no was my job and I didn't do it. I was afraid of being the person who lost Mars. She folded the paper again, smaller. I've run the root cause on my own decision for most of a year and let everybody think I was the one person in the building with no stake in it. The clock says three sixty six. Tomorrow it's a year. I can't do another day of it like that. I want it in the record. I'm not asking you to protect me. I'm asking you not to make it a story.

Sam didn't say anything for a while. He was thinking about a flight line in Arizona, and a form with his own signature on it, and the hour he hadn't taken. He didn't tell her. It wasn't hers to carry, and it was her night.
Thank you for telling me, he said. I'm going to sleep on what happens next. I'll call you in the morning.
She nodded. She gave him the paper. Then she went down the stairs ahead of him with one hand on the rail, and he watched her taillights all the way to the cattle guard.

At home there was a long white envelope on the mat, green ink, Golden postmark. Page nine. On the counter by the door, under his keys, his own envelope was where he'd left it, addressed to Ruth in his block capitals, unsealed. He set Hana's email next to it and opened Ruth's with the butter knife.
Ruth's Console Log, page nine: I said yes.

Ruth's console log, 15 days before launch. oh seven hundred, flight readiness review. bldg 4, room 210. open items 3. oh seven forty, items 1 and 3 closed. oh seven forty two, item 2. isol VLV 2, cycle 3, October 18. pending 7 months. oh seven forty five, prop recommends downgrade to crit 2. close UNR. two clean retests. no recurrence in flight valve checkout. oh seven fifty, Wendell: no recurrence because nobody has run it cold 500 times. asked for the shelf valve again. oh seven fifty two, administrator: the shelf valve is in Pueblo and the window is in june. oh eight hundred, a crit 1 open at this review needs a waiver. FD signs. oh eight fifteen, room waited. nobody said sign it. nobody had to. oh eight twenty, waiver 35-114. isol VLV 2 closed UNR at crit 2. lot life test waived. my signature. oh eight twenty one, Wendell left. didn't slam the door. worse. sixteen hundred, Lise at my console after the crew brief. asked if I was sure. sixteen oh one, I said yes. seventeen thirty, L minus 15. I said yes.

That's the page. I've read it more than any other page in the binder, and it's the shortest. Fifteen days before the Petrel left, I signed a waiver that let a valve fly with a question nobody had answered, and that afternoon the commander of the ship came to my console in her flight suit and asked me if I was sure. Lise Arnaud didn't ask many questions. When she did she meant them. I said yes. I said it the way you say it to a person you want to stop worrying, which is a different way from saying it because it's true.

I'm going to try to tell you what that morning was, because the useful part is the shape of it. Nobody in room 210 lied. Propulsion recommended what it believed. Wendell said what he knew. The Administrator said where the shelf valve was and where the window was, both of which were facts. The rule said a crit 1 item open at the review needed the flight director's signature, and it was a good rule, and it put the decision in exactly one pair of hands. Then the room waited. You can feel a room wait. Everybody in it had done their part honestly, and every honest part pointed the same direction, and the last pen was mine.

I could tell you the system did it, and I'd be telling you half of it. The system made saying yes easy. It made saying no expensive and lonely. I still chose. Both of those are true, and if you only ever let yourself say one of them you'll learn the wrong thing from your own worst day.

Page nine is B7, organizational change and culture, because culture is the thing that decides what a room does while it waits. It's people and conflict, because the hardest conversation on a program is the one where somebody tells you what they did. It's a chapter about silence, too, which I didn't plan. You'll have three weeks of it. Plan for it while you can still talk.

How the exam asks it. A waiver accepts a risk; it doesn't resolve it. The exam favors the answer that documents the risk, names who accepts it with the authority to, and keeps the data honest, over the answer that makes an open item quietly disappear.

One day somebody will stand in front of you and tell you the worst thing they did on your program. It might be a number they rounded, a test they skipped, a closure they talked a room into. What you do in the next minute decides whether anybody tells you anything again, so it's worth deciding now what you'll do.

Listen to the end. The Code's 3.2.3 asks you to actively listen to other points of view, seeking to understand them, and it's never harder than when the other point of view is a confession. Don't fix it while they're talking. Don't reassure them, either. Reassurance in that minute sounds like I'd rather you hadn't said it.

Thank them, and mean it. Then be exact about what happens next, and promise only what's yours to promise. The Code is plain about the facts. Responsibility, in 2.1, is our duty to take ownership for the decisions we make or fail to make, the actions we take or fail to take, and the consequences. When we make or discover errors or omissions, 2.2.5 says we take prompt corrective action, and its comment says we communicate them to the appropriate authority as soon as they're discovered. So a fact about a safety decision goes into the record, through the process that owns that record. The best way, by a long distance, is for the person to write it themselves, in their own words, under their own name. It's their account. Let it stay theirs.

Then protect the person who told you. Section 2.3.5: we don't retaliate against people for raising good faith ethical concerns. Its comment adds something people skip: we abstain from accusing others of ethical misconduct when we don't have all the facts. A confession gives you one person's part. It almost never gives you the room. If you turn one person's honesty into the whole explanation, you've done two wrong things at once. You've punished the only person who told you the truth, and you've told everybody else in the room they're safe as long as they keep quiet. The Code's honesty chapter has a line for it. When outcomes are negative, we avoid burying information or shifting blame to others. Making one engineer the face of an organization's decision is shifting blame with good paperwork.

There's a name for the way of thinking that holds both halves. A just culture asks what went wrong rather than who caused the problem. It isn't the same as a no blame culture. People are still accountable, and discipline is tied to the behavior, not to how bad the outcome was. An honest mistake is something the organization learns from; deliberate misconduct can still cost someone their job. James Reason wrote it down in 1997, about industrial accidents, and his point was practical. Without a just culture you don't get a reporting culture, and without a reporting culture you find out about your problems at the investigation.

One more thing, and it's a conflict of interest, which you've met in procurement. A person investigating a decision they made has a stake in the answer. That doesn't mean they come off the work. Often they're the one who knows it best. It means they disclose it, as 4.3.1 asks, and somebody independent checks the work alongside them. Keep the expert. Add the independence. Write both down.

How the exam asks it. When a team member admits a mistake: listen, thank them, get the facts into the proper record through the process (ideally in their own words), protect them from retaliation, and treat it as a system finding. Firing, public naming, and quiet burial are all distractors.

Projects live inside organizations, and organizations change their minds. A company merges two departments to save money, gets a new chief executive, reorganizes around a product, closes a building. Somebody upstairs drew a line on a chart, and now it's your project's problem. The ECO's B7 asks two things of you: assess the organization's culture, and evaluate what the change will do to the project and decide what you need to do about it. Both come before the announcement if you can get there in time, and at once if you can't.

Culture is easier to see than to name. Edgar Schein described three levels of it, sorted by how visible they are. Artifacts are what you can see and hear: the furniture, the dress code, the jokes people tell in the break room, the coffee can on the stand console with forty years of fingerprints on it. Espoused values are what the organization says about itself, on the wall and in the all hands. Underneath are the assumptions, the beliefs so deep nobody says them because nobody thinks they're beliefs. Schedule wins ties. The console belongs to whoever's qualified, whatever their badge says. You find the assumptions by watching what people do when two of the espoused values disagree.

A culture assessment is less formal than it sounds. Before a change lands, spend a week watching. Who gets interrupted in meetings, and by whom? What happens to the person who brings bad news? Which rules get followed when nobody's looking, and which only when somebody is? Ask a few people what would get someone fired here and what would get someone promoted, and listen for the gap between their answers and the poster. Write down the cultural norms you find, the ones that will help the change and the ones that will fight it. That list is the organizational culture you're really working in, and it's the one your plan has to survive.

The exam files culture under enterprise environmental factors, the conditions around the project you don't control but have to work inside: culture, structure, the market, the law, the weather on the stand. Its neighbor is organizational process assets, and people mix the two up. OPAs are what the organization hands you to use: its policies and procedures, templates, the lessons files from old projects, the change control and reporting procedures that say how a request gets approved and how often you report. A rough test. If you can open it, copy it, and use it, it's an OPA. If you can only work around it, it's an EEF. A gate review checklist is an OPA. The fact that nobody in the building wants to be the one who stops a test is an EEF, and it beats the checklist every time you let it.

When you merge two cultures, the artifacts are where the fights start and the assumptions are where they're decided. Two teams can share every espoused value on the poster and still have opposite answers to the question of who's allowed to stop the work.

There are models for leading change and you'll be asked about three. Kurt Lewin's is the oldest: unfreeze the old way, change, refreeze the new way so it holds. Critics have called it quaintly linear, and it is, and it's still right about the middle step being the short one. John Kotter's eight steps are the organizational version: create a sense of urgency, build a guiding coalition, form a strategic vision and initiatives, enlist a volunteer army, enable action by removing barriers, generate short term wins, sustain acceleration, and institute the change. Notice how much of that list is about other people's hands on the change.

Prosci's ADKAR, from Jeff Hiatt, is about the individual, and it's the one I'd keep in my pocket. A person changes when they have five things, in order. Awareness of the need for the change. Desire to take part in it and support it. Knowledge of what to do during and after. Ability to actually do it. Reinforcement, so it lasts. Prosci scores each one from 1 to 5, and the first one that comes out at three or below is the one you work on, because the later ones can't hold without it. Most stalled change is stuck at desire, and most organizations respond by running another training session, which is knowledge. You can't train somebody into wanting something.

Resistance is information. When a crew resists a change, they're telling you what they're afraid it will cost, and they're often right about at least one item. Ask what. Change the parts of the plan they're right about, and say so out loud, because a change people helped shape is one they can live in.

How the exam asks it. For organizational change, assess culture and the change's impact on the project first, then plan actions. If one person resists, diagnose which ADKAR element is missing before acting. Training only fixes knowledge and ability.

A merged team isn't a bigger team. It's a new team made of two old ones, and it will go back to forming whether anybody gives it permission or not. Bruce Tuckman's stages assume you start at the beginning once, but even good teams revert to earlier stages when circumstances change, and a change in leadership is the textbook trigger. Put two teams with two leads under one new lead, and you've got both. Expect the storming. Plan for it.

Storming has sources, and naming them helps. The usual list is short: schedules, priorities, resources, technical opinions, procedures, cost, and personalities, and personality clashes cause less of it than most people think. When two crews merge, the sources of conflict are usually competing priorities and scarce resources dressed up as personality. Two leads want the same test stand on the same Thursday, and each crew decides the other one is difficult. Ask what the argument is about, in one sentence, before you decide who's being difficult. Most of the time the honest sentence is about a stand, a date, or a rule, and those you can fix.

Then read how hot it is. Speed Leas, who studied conflict in congregations, described five levels: a problem to solve, then disagreement, then contest, then fight or flight, and at the top a conflict where people want the other side gone. At the bottom people talk about the problem. Further up the talk moves to the people, then to winning, then to who's on whose side. Conflict resolution starts with knowing which level you're on. Read the context of the conflict before you pick a move. A disagreement over a stand schedule wants a whiteboard and twenty minutes. A level four fight wants you to separate the people from the problem, meet them one at a time, and maybe bring in somebody neutral. Using a level one tool on a level four fight is how a manager makes things worse while trying to be nice about it.

Start with purpose. People who used to answer to different leads need a reason to be one group that's bigger than the chart. Write the team's purpose with the team, from the project's vision, in words they'd say in a break room. The ECO's P1 says help ensure a shared vision, promote it, and keep it current, and when it's misunderstood, find out why. A vision two crews don't share is usually a vision one of them never got to say out loud.

Writing it once isn't enough. A vision statement on the wall fades into the paint inside a month. You keep it alive by using it. Communicate the vision at the top of the meetings that matter, tie a hard call back to it out loud, and ask a new person to say it back to you in their own words. If they can't, you've learned how well it's been carried. And revisit the vision when the world under it moves. A merger, a new customer, a lost window, each is a reason to ask whether the old words still point the right way. Vision drift is quiet. The team keeps working hard toward something the project stopped being two months ago. Changing the words openly, with the team, is cheaper than finding out at a review that half of them have been building last year's project.

Then a team charter. The charter is the what and the why: purpose, values, how the team decides, how it handles conflict, how it communicates, what done means. Ground rules are the how, the specific working agreements, written by the team and specific enough to break: bad news inside the shift; nobody goes out alone; disagree with the data before the person. When a rule is broken, deal with it promptly and privately first.

Put the conflict management approach in that charter in plain words, and show it to people outside the team too. Inside, it says what healthy conflict looks like here: argue about the data in the room, not about people in the hallway; if two people can't settle it in a day it goes to the lead, and if the lead can't, to you. Outside, the customer and the other departments need to know where a disagreement goes, so a supplier with a complaint about one of your engineers brings it to you and not to a vice president. Constructive conflict is how a team finds what one person missed. You write down how conflict will be handled to keep it constructive, not to make it rare.

Then roles, and here's where merged teams fall apart, in the seams. Who signs a cryogenic operations permit now? Who approves overtime? Who can stop a test? A responsibility assignment matrix, a RACI, puts the work down the side and the roles across the top, and for each line marks who's Responsible for doing it, who's Accountable for it, who's Consulted, and who's Informed. The rule that does the work: one accountable person per line. Two accountable people means nobody is. A line with no A is a decision that will be made by whoever's standing closest.

Count the channels while you're at it. With n people, the communication channels are n times n minus 1, over 2. Two teams of 11 and 7 talking among themselves and through their leads have 77. Put all 18 in one huddle and you have 153. Structure brings it down: crews with leads, and a leads' huddle, and you're near 50 again. A merged team that meets as one big room every morning is paying for the merger twice.

And then the people. Emotional intelligence is a contested idea with a useful core. Daniel Goleman made it famous in 1995, and the research on it is mixed, but the core holds up in any break room: notice what you feel before you act on it, manage it, notice what other people feel, and use that to work with them. In a merger that means noticing that the angriest person in the room is usually the most frightened one, and that what they're frightened of is often specific.

Psychological safety is the belief that you won't be punished or humiliated for speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns, or mistakes. After someone confesses something in front of a team, everybody in the room is watching to find out what speaking up costs here. That's the moment you build it or lose it. The Code says the same thing in its own words in 5.2.5: we strive to create an environment in which others feel safe to tell the truth.

Last, coaching and mentoring, which the ECO puts under P5. Coaching is focused on a specific task or objective: running your first merged huddle, writing your first permit delegation. Mentoring is broader and longer, someone with more experience helping a mentee grow. A new lead of a merged team needs both, and needs to know which one she's getting on a given afternoon.

How the exam asks it. A merged team returns to forming: re-establish purpose, a team charter, and clear roles with the team. Channels n(n minus 1) 2. One A per RACI line. A request for help with a specific upcoming task is coaching.

About every twenty six months, Mars passes almost behind the Sun as we see it, and for some days the radio link between Earth and Mars goes bad. The plasma near the Sun scrambles signals. Mission controllers' practice, for the robots, is not to send commands at all for a stretch around it, because a spacecraft acting on a corrupted command is worse than a spacecraft doing nothing. Data still trickles back, with bits lost and resent. And the vehicles stay active, carrying out commands sent in advance. Teams spend weeks getting ready.

That sentence, carrying out commands sent in advance, is the whole lesson. A planned communications blackout is an impediment you can see coming, with a start date and an end date. You don't manage it during. You manage it before.

Start with the schedule. Find every activity that needs the far side during the silence: an answer, a sign off, a test, a data set. The ECO's R8 asks you to coordinate with other projects and operations, and the far side is operations. Pull forward what can move. Push the rest past the end, using float you've counted, not float you've hoped for. What can do neither becomes a decision someone has to make without you.

The far side isn't the only schedule you're tangled up with. Most projects share people, test stands, ranges, and data with other projects and with operations, and those links are external dependencies: activities in your plan that wait on somebody else's. Put each one in your schedule as a milestone with an owner on the other side, and check them on a cadence, not when they're late. On a program the projects' schedules roll up into one integrated master schedule, so a slip in one shows up in the others the same day instead of next quarter. Agile teams do the same thing out loud with a scrum of scrums, one person from each team meeting a few times a week to say what's blocking whom. The move doesn't change. Coordinate with operations and the other projects before you need them, because the stand they promised you is the one they'll lend to somebody louder.

So write the decision rights down. For each decision that might come up during the silence, who decides, what their limits are, and what they do if they're outside them. Then hand the authority over with the decision, the way you'd hand a deputy a signature card. The people on the far side will decide anyway, because they have to. The only question is whether they'll be guessing at what you'd have wanted.

Then triggers. A risk has a trigger condition, the observable thing that means it's happening. During a silence your observations are thin, so pick triggers you'll actually be able to see: a status word that changes, a beacon that misses a slot. Name the owner of each response. The moment a trigger fires, the response starts, and if the risk has actually happened, it's now an issue. The ECO's B4 wants you to recognize that moment and act on it, not argue about whether it counts.

Then a communications plan for no communications. Who hears what, from whom, when the line closes; what you'll publish during, if anything comes through; when and how the first real word after will reach the people waiting for it. People can sit through a silence they were told about. What wrecks them is a silence that nobody explained.
And send what matters before the line. The last message before a long quiet is the one people read twenty times.

How the exam asks it. For a known future outage: identify dependent activities, pull forward or resequence them, delegate decision rights in advance with limits and triggers, and communicate the plan to stakeholders before it starts.

Some of the people who'll feel the silence most aren't on your team. They're the customers and the families and the public, and the ECO's P6 asks you to identify what they expect, align the outcome with it where you can, and watch for the moment their expectations and the facts part ways. They will part ways. When they do, go to them. People forgive a lot from someone who stood in the wind and told them. They forgive very little from a press release.

Customers aren't a single group, and their expectations aren't a single list. You have internal and external customers: the operations crew that will inherit what you build is a customer as much as the agency that pays for it. Find out what each one expects, early and in their words, and write it next to what you're actually delivering. Then keep checking, because customer expectations move while you work. The cheap ways are the best ones. A demo every few weeks, a two question satisfaction survey after each delivery, ten minutes on the phone asking what's changed. Track customer satisfaction the way you track cost. Customer feedback that says the gap is growing is a trigger, like a reading on a gauge. Close it with a conversation and, if it's needed, a change request. Don't close it by hoping.

Stakeholder expectations usually collide before they reach you. The families expect one thing, the agency another, the crew a third, and each group is sure the others agree with it. Sort them by group first, and put each group's expectations in the open, side by side. Then facilitate rather than announce: get the people who disagree into one conversation, show them the same facts, and look for the outcome each can live with. You won't always align expectations completely. You can always make sure nobody is surprised by what the others were promised.

And the outside world keeps changing while you plan. A new technology, a regulator, a market, a government. B8 asks you to survey those changes and assess what each one does to your scope or backlog, and to keep doing it. Most changes in the outside world do nothing to your project this month. A few change what's possible next year. The skill is telling which is which, quickly and honestly, and putting the second kind where somebody with the authority to act on it will see it.

Keep doing it means a habit, not a meeting. Horizon scanning is the habit: once a month somebody reads past the edge of the project for external changes, a rule out for comment, a supplier's quarterly report, a competitor's announcement, and writes a line on each. Trend analysis is what you do with the lines. One supplier missing a date is news. Three suppliers in the same region missing dates over six months is a trend. It goes in the risk register, and you may need to reprioritize the backlog around it. Say a regulator posts a draft rule that would add a test you don't have time for. It isn't final. You still assess it now: what it adds to scope, when it could take effect, who decides whether to plan for it. That ongoing review, written down, is the difference between a surprise and a change you were ready for.

How the exam asks it. When stakeholders' expectations and the facts diverge, engage them directly and early with what you know, what you don't, and when they'll hear more. For an external change, assess its impact on scope and backlog before acting.

Lise asked me if I was sure. I've had twenty seven years to work out what I should have said, and it isn't no, which would have been as much of a performance as yes. It's, No, I'm not. Here's what I'd need to be, and here's what it would cost, and here's who should decide whether it's worth it. That's all a flight director has to offer anybody. An honest account of what she doesn't know.

Somebody's going to tell you something this spring. Then the line will close, and you won't be able to say anything to the person you most want to talk to for three weeks. Make sure the last thing you told her was true.
How the exam asks it. Honest uncertainty beats false confidence. When asked whether something is safe and you don't know, say what you know, what you'd need, and who decides.

Saturday, February 18. 6:50 AM. He hadn't slept much. Page nine was on the kitchen table, and Hana's email beside it, and the two of them said the same thing twenty four years apart in different typefaces.
At 6:52 his phone lit up. Hana. I haven't slept. Tell me what happens now.
AR 2207 had been open since last February, on his signature, and Hana had run it since. Every root cause meeting for a year had started with her at the whiteboard.

He wrote down what he knew. The closure record already said RECOMMENDED BY: PROPULSION. Bea's account at the hardware store said somebody said can we. Work order 59-3318 said the third attempt was cancelled. What nobody had written down was that the somebody was Hana, or that she'd decided the night before and written it up to make the case. It was a fact about how a safety decision got made, and the board was reviewing AR 2207 in March.

Under it he wrote what that told him about how Tallgrass decided. A recommendation written the night before a review. A room that waited for the person whose valve it was. A contractor who found out from a work order. Nobody had lied, and the place had still learned to close what it wasn't sure of. Whatever he did this morning, both buildings would read it as the answer to what telling the truth cost here.
He was aware, writing it, that he'd once sat in a hotel bathroom at two in the morning deciding whether to round. He hadn't. It had been close.
Over the high bay doors, twenty miles east, the clock would say 365 by now. He called her at 7:05.
Hana's message asks what happens now. How should Sam respond?
A. Ask Hana to add her account to AR 2207's closure history, and disclose her stake in the review.
B. Move the root cause lead on Monday to an engineer with no history on the valve or the 2059 room.
C. Refer the 2059 closure to Tallgrass HR and the ARA's ethics office for a formal inquiry.
D. Keep what she's told him between the two of them, and let her carry on leading the root cause.

He thanks her first. Then he tells her what happens, in order. On Monday she writes her account as an addendum to AR 2207's closure history, in her own words, and it goes to the anomaly board and the readiness board's clerk. In the same note she discloses that she's investigating a decision she helped make. Sam asks the ARA's mission assurance office for a propulsion engineer from outside Tallgrass to check the root cause work alongside her, and says in writing that she stays its lead. He tells her he won't let anyone punish her for telling the truth, as far as that's his to stop, and that he'll say so in writing. Past the record, he won't tell anyone. Whether her team hears it from her, and when, is hers. A long pause. That's it? That's the start of it. On Monday at 4:10 the addendum is in the file, two pages, signed H. IWASAKI.

That's a go. Responsibility means owning the decision and getting the fact to the appropriate authority, best in the person's own words. Disclose the conflict of interest and add independence without throwing away her expertise, and make sure telling the truth costs her nothing.
Tuesday, February 28. 4:30 PM. Garrett's memo came to Sam forty eight hours before the all hands, which Garrett's assistant said was a courtesy.

TALLGRASS AEROSPACE OFFICE OF THE CEO ORGANIZATION ANNOUNCEMENT (DRAFT, FOR RELEASE THURSDAY, MARCH 2). Effective Monday, April 3, 2062, Halcyon Vehicle Integration, 48 people, and Propulsion Test, 19, combine as one Integration and Test team of 67, led by Corinne Mathers. One management structure. One technician pool. One shift schedule. This change supports the efficiency goals set by our investor board on February 22 and positions Tallgrass for the launch campaign.

Corinne came to his office ten minutes later with the same memo. She'd taken over the high bay from him in January of last year, and she still sometimes caught herself calling it his. She was forty four, ran the building's crane certifications in her head, and had never once worked at the stand. I found out yesterday, she said. I've got two days to tell nineteen people they work for me, and I've never chilled a line in my life.

The savings were Tallgrass's own, in its overhead. The program's baseline wouldn't move. The program's work would. Stand 2 still had flight work until the stage shipped in July. Building 6 was running the second test article's life test seven nights a week. And the root cause team drew on both buildings.
Garrett called at five. It's done, Sam. I'm telling you as a courtesy. Don't make it a project.
Garrett is merging the stand and integration teams and says not to make it a project. What should Sam do?
A. Ask Corinne to draw up the new structure this week, ready for Thursday's announcement.
B. Ask Garrett to postpone the merger until the stage ships in July and the stand's flight work is done.
C. Walk both buildings with Corinne on Wednesday to assess the merger's effect on the program's work.
D. Let Thursday's announcement go out as written, and work its effects on the program as they come.

He, Corinne, and Quinn walk both buildings on Wednesday. In the high bay the artifacts are laminated checklists and a whiteboard that says DAYS SINCE LAST CRANE STOP. At the stand they're a coffee can on the console older than Corinne, and a rule nobody wrote down: the console belongs to whoever's qualified, and nobody else touches it, whatever their badge says. The high bay's assumption is that the schedule wins ties. The stand's is that the data does. They write the impacts down: life test coverage, cryogenic permit authority, the stage's ship date, root cause staffing. Then the required actions. Console and permit authority stay with qualified stand people, and Hana keeps technical authority over propulsion tests. The stand's night shift doesn't change until the stage ships. Corinne gets a stand mentor. Sam takes the list to Garrett at seven on Wednesday night. Garrett reads it, crosses out nothing, and says, Fine. The date stays. Yes, sir. Thursday's memo has four new lines.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Supporting organizational change starts with assessing the culture and evaluating the change's impact on the project, then determining the actions it requires and bringing them to the decision makers before it lands.

Monday, March 13. 7:00 AM. Sixty seven people in the high bay, which was the only room big enough, standing among the work stands under the departure stage's empty cradle. The stand crew stood together near the doors, in insulated coveralls, as if they might need to leave.

Thursday's memo had said the stand's night shift stayed as it was until July, and that console and permit authority stayed with qualified stand people. The stand crew had read those four lines more than the rest of it.
Corinne had asked Sam to say something. She'd also asked him not to say much. She had a whiteboard on wheels and a marker in each hand.

Arlo Dunn was at the front of the stand group, cap with the ear flaps, arms folded. He'd come in off a night shift and hadn't been home. Beside him Wendell had found a stool somewhere and was sitting on it with his hearing protection around his neck, looking at the empty cradle.
Somebody in the high bay group said, not quite quietly enough, that at least the stand people would learn to read a schedule.
Someone just took a dig at the stand crew. How should Sam bring the two groups together?
A. Hand out the program vision and a team charter that he and Corinne drafted last week.
B. Ask the merged team to write its own purpose and working agreements from the program's vision.
C. Open with the investor board's goals and Garrett's savings figures for the merger.
D. Let each former team keep its own norms, and reconcile them after the stage ships in July.

Sam says three sentences: why the ship matters, why this team matters to the ship, and that he doesn't know yet what this team is for in its own words, and they do. Then he gives Corinne the floor. It takes three sessions, on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, in mixed groups of six. The purpose they write is one line. Ship the stage in July with every question about it answered, and keep the stand honest until we do. The working agreements fill the rest of the board. The console belongs to the qualified. Anybody can call a hold, and nobody gets asked why in front of the room. Disagree with the data before the person. Bad news inside the shift. Arlo writes the last one himself, in capitals: NOBODY GOES OUT ALONE. They agree to look at all of it again the week the stage ships.

Exactly right. A shared vision is built with the people who have to hold it, from the project's vision, in their own words, and kept current. A team that writes its purpose and its working agreements is a team that has started agreeing to be one.
Friday, March 17. 8:00 AM. The board had sat on Wednesday, downtown, in the federal building with the bad coffee. Ruth had been on the bench. Sam had watched the feed from the program room.

The first item was the ARA's margin model. The board found that it credited six spare stacks that had been installed in 2060, directed the ARA's mission assurance office to rebuild the model from the station's plant log, and asked for it at the July session. Until then, the minutes said, the ARA's figure would carry a footnote: UNDER BOARD REVIEW. The second item was AR 2207. The board asked Tallgrass for the anomaly's full closure history, who recommended what and when, by its next session.
Hana's addendum was already in the file. Two pages, signed. The board's clerk had acknowledged it in one line.
Garrett came in at eight and shut the door. He was in a good mood, which was the thing to watch.

Here's how this goes away, he said. The record says propulsion recommended the closure. Hana says it was her. She's a grown woman. Our statement to the board says the engineer who recommended it has owned it, we name her, she keeps her job, and we look like a company that tells the truth. September 2059 is history. Nobody else needs to be in that room.
Garrett wants a statement naming Hana as the engineer behind the closure. How should Sam respond?
A. Turn Garrett down in private, and send the board the complete closure history it asked for.
B. Turn down Garrett's plan at Monday's leads meeting, with all fourteen leads in the room.
C. Leave the choice to Hana, and back whatever she decides to do about the statement.
D. Agree to Garrett's statement, naming Hana as the engineer who recommended the closure.

He says it across the desk, in a level voice. No, sir. The board asked for the history. It'll get all of it. Who was in the room, the work order, Hana's account in her own words, and what made closing it feel reasonable to everyone at the table. No single name as the story. Garrett's smile holds. You're telling me it was me. No, sir. I don't know that, and I won't say it. I'm telling you it was a room, and the board should see the room. A long pause. Then Garrett stands up. Send it, he says, and goes. Quinn builds the history over the weekend from the calendar, the work order, Bea's account where Bea has agreed to it, and Hana's. It goes to the clerk on Tuesday with a cover page that lists causes, not culprits: a review date treated as fixed, a closure category that let a crit 1 question leave the books, and a third attempt cancelled because the stand was wanted elsewhere.

That's a go. Address the disagreement directly and privately, don't accuse anyone without the facts, and give governance the complete record rather than one person's part of it. Accountability without a scapegoat is the whole room's history, told straight.
Wednesday, March 22. Corinne's cross training sign up sheet had been on the blockhouse door for nine days. It had space for nineteen names. It had none.

Everybody on the stand crew had been to both briefings. Every one of them could tell you what the merger was, when it started, and what the new shift schedule looked like. Corinne had scheduled a third briefing for Friday, with slides.

Wendell had told Quinn, who had told Sam, that Wendell had turned seventy last August and was a contractor, and that the day somebody from the high bay sat his console without his say so would be his last day. He'd said it quietly. Quinn had believed him.

Sam went out at seven, before the night shift started. Arlo Dunn, who had the stand that night, was in the blockhouse with his boots up, eating a sandwich out of wax paper. Last time the schedule ran this stand, they cancelled Wendell's third attempt, he said, before Sam asked anything. That's what everybody out here knows about 2059. So you'll understand.
On the blockhouse wall, above the coffee can, somebody had taped up a photo of the high bay's whiteboard from the charter session. NOBODY GOES OUT ALONE was circled.
Corinne's cross training sheet has been up for nine days with no names on it. What's Sam's best move?
A. Tell the stand crew the merger is final, and note cross training sign ups in annual reviews.
B. Talk with the stand crew one at a time to find which part of the change is stuck.
C. Add more training on the new structure, starting with Corinne's third briefing on Friday.
D. Exempt the stand crew from the merger until the stage ships in July, and let the high bay go first.

It takes most of a week, a coffee at a time. Awareness, fine. Knowledge, fine; they could teach the briefing. Ability, fine. Asked to score each step from one to five, almost everyone gives desire a one, and every one of them gives the same reason in different words: the merger looks like the schedule taking the stand, and the last time it did, a valve flew with a question in it. So Sam fixes the cause. The charter's console rule goes into the team's written procedures, signed by Corinne and Hana, with Wendell as the authority on who's qualified. Cross training becomes Wendell's program, on his terms: high bay technicians learn the stand from the people who run it, and nobody touches the console until Wendell signs them off. Wendell reads the procedure twice and says, Who wrote this? Corinne. Hana checked it. He grunts. On Monday the sheet has fourteen names, and the first is Arlo's.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Change works person by person, through awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement, the steps called ADKAR. Find the first weak one, here desire, and address its cause rather than its symptom. Resistance is information. Changing the part of the plan the crew was right about is what makes the change one they can live in.
Tuesday, March 28. 6:30 AM. The stand crew's huddle was fifteen minutes at the blockhouse, standing up, before the morning chilldown. Hana came on Tuesdays.

On Monday afternoon Hana had told the stand crew herself, in the blockhouse, in about two minutes, standing up. She'd said what she'd said in the room in September 2059, and that she'd written it into the record, and that she was still running the root cause, with a reviewer from the agency checking her work. Then she'd gone back to her desk. She'd told Sam afterward that it was the worst two minutes of her life, and that she'd timed it.

This morning Hana went through the overnight data, as usual. When she finished, Arlo spoke before anybody could move. So the stand did its job in 2059, and the office closed it anyway, and the office was you.

Nobody said anything. One of the four high bay techs on early rotation, a woman near the back, said, She wasn't the office. She was the one who told us. Two of the stand techs looked at her as if she'd taken a side, which she had.

Hana stood there with the data sheet. Her hands were steady, which Sam had learned meant something. Wendell took his hearing protection off his neck, folded it, put it in his pocket, and walked to his truck.
The huddle turned on Hana, and Wendell just walked to his truck. What should Sam do right now?
A. Let the argument run in the huddle, as the merged team's storming stage.
B. Close the subject in the huddle, and keep the huddle to today's work from now on.
C. Move Hana's updates to written reports for a few weeks while things settle.
D. End the huddle, and talk with Arlo and Wendell privately before anything else.

He ends the huddle with one sentence and goes to Wendell's truck. Wendell is sitting with the engine off. After a while he says the third attempt was his, and that he'd chilled the stand on the Sunday night for it, and that when the work order changed he didn't fight it, because he was a contractor, and contractors don't fight. I wasn't in that room. I knew where it was. Arlo, at lunch, says he's angry at a room and Hana was the only person in it standing where he could see her. On Thursday Corinne runs an hour in the blockhouse with the door shut. Hana says one thing: that she'd rather be asked than talked about. Wendell says his part. The team adds a line to its working agreements: We talk about decisions, not about people. Anybody can ask anybody why. Arlo asks Hana a question about cycle 3 data on Friday, in the huddle, out loud. She answers it.

Exactly right. Identify the real source of the conflict and its context before working it: here, anger at an organizational decision landing on the one person who owned up. Talk privately first, then help the team agree on how to handle it, so psychological safety survives the confession.

Monday, April 10. Integration and Test had existed for one week. Corinne had kept a list of what had broken, on a legal pad, and by Monday morning it ran to the bottom of the second page. She put it on Sam's desk without a word and sat down across from him.

The company's personnel system had moved the stand technicians under the high bay's shift supervisors, and only stand leads were qualified to sign cryogenic operations permits. On Thursday night nobody on shift could sign one, and a chilldown had been scrubbed at the gate. The second test article's life test in Building 6 had lost a night, its first since November.
Badge access had been reset for everyone in the new team. Four high bay technicians on stand rotation couldn't get through the stand's gate, and two stand technicians couldn't get into Building 6.
Overtime requests for all sixty seven people now went to Corinne. She had forty one waiting.

And the new shift schedule had put the stand's night crew on the high bay's rotating shifts starting May 1, which the memo had said wouldn't happen until July. Somebody in scheduling hadn't read the memo.
I can do all of it, Corinne said. I can't do all of it today.
Corinne has a long list of merger problems and can't do them all today. How should Sam handle the list?
A. Log every item, and work them through together at the merged team's monthly review.
B. Fix the badge problem himself tonight, and take the rest of the list as each item comes up.
C. Ask Garrett to hold the merger for the stand crew until the problems are fixed.
D. Rank the list with Corinne by its impact on the stage and the life test, and give each an owner.

They rank it together in twenty minutes. The permit gap is first, because it stops work every night. By two o'clock Hana has signed an interim delegation naming the three qualified stand leads as permit signers on any shift, whoever they report to on paper, and HR has a ticket to fix the system properly by the end of the month. The shift change goes second; Quinn takes it to scheduling, and the stand's night crew comes off the May 1 rotation until the stage ships. Badges go to Corinne by Wednesday. Overtime goes to the shift leads, with authority to approve up to a cap and send anything over it to Corinne. Sam writes the four owners and dates on her legal pad, and they agree to look at the list again every Friday until it's empty. On Friday it has one line left.

That's a go. Evaluate the impact of each impediment, prioritize, apply an intervention strategy with clear owners, and reassess continually. When a risk like the permit authority becomes an issue, act on it the same day.

Tuesday, April 18. Countdown to Ares ran it as the lead item on Monday night. A company called Sundog Relay, eighteen months old, with a ground station in New Mexico and a very good animation, announced that it would put a relay spacecraft in an orbit well off the line between Earth and Mars, where it could pass messages around the Sun when the Sun was in the way. No more conjunction blackouts, the animation said.

By Tuesday morning Families of Ares had a petition with forty thousand names on it. It asked the ARA to rent Sundog's relay, or to put a relay on Halcyon, so families could hear from the station during the silence. Frances Odum, who chaired the group, had sent it to Sam personally, with one line: Is this real?
Gwen Talley, Hale's chief of staff, called at nine. The Director would like to know whether Halcyon can carry one of these. Or whether we can buy time on theirs. Before May, ideally.

Rafa had already read Sundog's regulatory filing, because Rafa read filings for fun. He came in with it folded open. First launch no earlier than late 2063, it said. Operational in 2064, if everything worked the first time, which, Rafa said, it wouldn't.
Commander Yusra Haddad, the release backlog's product owner, had the next review on Thursday.
Rafa has Sundog's filing for a relay that could fly in 2064. What should Sam do about it?
A. Have Rafa and Quinn work out what the relay changes for Halcyon before anyone answers Frances.
B. Set the relay aside as outside Halcyon's baselined scope, and keep Thursday's review as planned.
C. Ask the ARA to sign a letter of intent with Sundog this week, ahead of the silence.
D. Ask Hana to find room in the cargo module's mass margin for a small relay spacecraft.

Rafa and Quinn take a day. Sundog can't help this May; it doesn't exist yet. The next conjunction, in July 2064, falls after Halcyon reaches Mars, and a relay could matter then, to the station and to whatever ship comes next. It doesn't belong in Halcyon's scope, and Halcyon's cargo has no room for it anyway. So it's parked outside the release backlog, on the ARA's opportunity list, with Rafa's note on what the station's radios would need: a relay interface study after arrival. Yusra sees it on Thursday and leaves it there. Sam calls Frances at noon. It's real, ma'am. It isn't real yet. Nothing can carry a log around the Sun this May. I'm sorry. Here's what you will hear, and when. She's quiet for a moment. That's the first straight answer anybody's given me about it.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Survey external changes such as new technology, assess and prioritize their impact on scope and backlog, and route opportunities outside your scope to whoever can use them. Then tell the people with expectations about it the truth, early.

Wednesday, May 3. Quinn had drawn the line on the integrated plan in red marker, top to bottom across every sheet: Thursday, May 25, 4:15 PM. Twenty two days later, a second line. Between them she'd shaded the plan gray, and the gray covered more than anybody had expected.

The ARA's rule was simple. While Mars was within three degrees of the Sun, nothing personal went either way, no commands went to the station, and the relay network carried only a short station status beacon, once a sol, repeated until it got through.

Quinn had found eleven activities inside the gray that needed something from Mars. The largest was the cargo manifest. It closed on Thursday, June 1, and the station had to sign off the bridge stacks' mounting interface and the cutover procedure that used them before it could. Two joint bench runs of the Breather's control code on the station's bench were scheduled for June 7 and June 14. The cutover inventory needed the station's count. Rafa's next release demo used bench data.
Six of them can move ahead of the line if the station can take them, she said. Three can go after it if we spend float we've actually got. Two can't do either.
One way light time was twenty and a half minutes. Every question to the station took a sol to come back, and the answer came from Chiamaka Okonkwo, who ran Breather operations on the station.
Quinn found eleven activities in the gray that need something from Mars. How should Sam handle them?
A. Keep the plan as it stands, and let the station catch up on its items after June 17.
B. Close the manifest on June 1 on Earth's data, and have the station confirm it after the silence.
C. Ask the station which of the eleven items it can take before the line, and resequence the rest.
D. Ask the station's engineers to work extra shifts to answer all eleven items before May 25.

Quinn sends the list to the station in the morning packet with the reason for each date. Chiamaka's answer comes back the next sol. Q1 understood as: Earth wants our answers before we can't give them. Yes. Bench run moved to Sol 3994 and 3995. Interface sign off by Sol 3999. The bench runs move to May 15 and 16. The station signs off the bridge stacks' interface and the cutover procedure on May 19, a week before the line. Three activities move to the week of June 19, inside float Quinn has counted twice. The last two, the station's own plant decisions and what Rafa's release does without bench data, go to Sam's list for decision rights. Quinn redraws the gray, and it's smaller.

Exactly right. Coordinating with operations means finding the dependent work, sequencing it around a known constraint, and agreeing it with the people on the other end. Pull forward, resequence on real float, and turn what's left into decisions to delegate.

Wednesday, May 17. Quinn's draft decision matrix was one page. Down the side, the decisions that might come up in twenty two days of silence. Across the top, the people who might make them: Hollis Bayne as station director, Chiamaka as Breather operations, Sam, the ARA's mission operations, the ARA's public affairs office, and the leads. In the boxes, R, A, C, and I.

It had problems, and she knew it, which was why it said DRAFT across the top in red. Two decisions had two people accountable. Two had nobody. One box said TBD in her handwriting, with a question mark after it, which was the most honest thing on the page.

Thandi Mokoena, who ran the agency's independent software checks, had sent one line, copied to Rafa: No Breather code goes onto the station bench during conjunction. Nobody can watch it. Rafa had replied with a thumbs up and, a minute later, a second message: agreed, annoyingly.
The autonomy release had its own line on the draft. Nobody expected to need it in June. Quinn had put it there because the uncrewed option was on the plan, and things on the plan got a line.
Two decisions were left over from the schedule: what the station could do with the old plant on its own authority, and what Earth would do if the beacon showed trouble.
Chiamaka's question from the morning packet sat at the top of Sam's screen. Q3 from us: during conjunction, who decides?
Some decisions are still left over from the schedule. How should Sam answer Chiamaka?
A. Keep every decision with Earth, and ask the station to hold anything significant until June.
B. Let each team decide whatever comes up in the silence as it arises, and sort it out in June.
C. Fix the matrix so each decision in the silence has one accountable owner and a trigger.
D. Give Hollis, as station director, authority over every decision for the length of the silence.

They fix the page in an afternoon. Every decision gets exactly one A. The station decides the station: old plant maintenance, stack actions, and rationing are Hollis's to approve and Chiamaka's to do, logged in numbered packets that go out the moment the line opens. The manifest is Sam's. Families' communications are the ARA public affairs office's, with Sam consulted and the beacon published unedited every sol. Breather code loads aren't anybody's: the line says FROZEN, and Thandi signs it. Then the triggers, each with an owner. If the beacon's plant word goes amber for two sols running, the ARA's mission operations convenes the board's duty member. If the beacon misses three slots, the same. Sam sends it in the morning packet with a note that Earth's job in the silence is to be ready, not to steer. Chiamaka's answer comes back the next sol. Q3 understood as: during conjunction, the station decides the station. Thank you. We were going to anyway. Now it's written down.

That's a go. For a known blackout, delegate decision rights in advance, with one accountable owner per decision, explicit limits, and trigger conditions that hand off the response. Put the authority with the people who'll be able to act.

Sunday, May 21. 6:40 PM. The wind had been at thirty five since noon, and it was carrying dust off the fields east of the campus in long brown sheets. Families of Ares had been at the main gate since four. About sixty people, in coats, with photographs in plastic sleeves taped to sticks, and candles in mason jars that kept going out and being lit again.

Security had called at five. So had Garrett. Have them moved to the county road. It's a liability. Hale's office had sent a statement for public affairs to read. It was three paragraphs long and said the ARA was committed.

Sam could see the gate from the program room window. He could see Frances Odum at the front, in the red coat, holding a photograph against her chest with both arms the way she had at the briefing in February of last year.
She'd called him in April about the relay. He'd told her the truth then. She'd brought the petition anyway, because forty thousand people had signed it.
In four days the line would close. Ada's last log would come in on Thursday morning, if it came. Malik Odum worked her night shift.
Frances and the families are holding a vigil outside. What should Sam do?
A. Have security move the vigil to the county road, and send public affairs to read the statement.
B. Promise the families a short message from every colonist before the line closes Thursday.
C. Invite Frances in for a private briefing in the conference room while the vigil goes on.
D. Walk down to the gate and talk with Frances and the families where they're standing.

He walks down without a coat, which he regrets in the first minute. Frances doesn't say anything at first. Then she says the thing she came to say: the families heard about the silence from a feed, the margin is under review and nobody's told them what that means, and they'd like to know what they'll get for twenty two days. So he tells them. A status beacon once a sol, posted unedited the hour it comes in: plant, power, life support, medical, and a line from the director. No personal logs either way. First logs after June 17, probably the day after. The margin has two numbers right now, the station's and the agency's, and the board will settle it in July. A man asks whether the beacon would say if something was wrong. It would say something changed. It wouldn't say what. I'm sorry. That's what it's built to do. Frances looks at him for a while. You'll have the same twenty two days I will. Yes, ma'am. She hands him the binder with the petition in it, and one of the jars, which has gone out.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Managing stakeholder expectations means identifying what they expect, telling them where the facts differ, and monitoring and responding in person when it matters. Say what they'll get, when, and its limits, before the silence starts.
Thursday, May 25. 5:40 AM. The two note chime. She was about as far away as she'd ever been.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 4004. One way, 21 minutes 1 second. Margin, 460 days. Hi, Dad. Log twenty four. Last one before the Sun. Comms says the line closes at twenty two fifteen UT, which is your Thursday afternoon. After that nothing personal goes either way until the Sun moves over. Twenty two days. The beacon goes every sol. If you see MED change, it's somebody's ankle. It's always somebody's ankle. Chiamaka printed Earth's list of who decides what and taped it to the plant room door. Mostly it says us. She says it's the first time Earth has written down something we already knew, and she said it like it was a compliment, which from her it is. Stack three's manifold is weeping again. She wants to pull it during the quiet, while nobody on Earth can have a meeting about it. I'm on her crew. Don't worry. I'm saying that knowing you will. Malik says to tell you the jalapeño plants are taller than him now. They're not. He's sitting down. The other place is fine. I'll tell you about it when there's more to tell, and there will be. Okay. I've got one thing to say and I'm going to say it once, because I rehearsed it in the shower and there's a timer on the shower. For twenty two days I won't hear your voice, so I won't be able to tell which one it is. All I'll have is the last one. You've been straight with me for a long time now. I've noticed. I'm asking anyway. If you're lying to me, I'll know when the ship's late. Don't make me find out that way. 460. Same minus nine. Love you. Log twenty four. See you on the other side of the Sun. Ada out.
He watched it twice. The second time he stopped it on her face just before she said the one thing she'd rehearsed, and sat there with his coffee in both hands.

The last uplink slot for personal traffic closed at 2:00 PM. He had eight hours. He had the root cause still open and the task order working, the stage due to ship in July, a margin with two numbers and a footnote, a merged team that had stopped shouting at itself sometime in April, and a program room with a red line drawn on every sheet of its plan.
At one fifteen he sat down at the kitchen table, in his own chair, and pressed record.
Sam has one last log before the silence. What should he tell Ada?
A. Send her the program's official monthly status report as his last message.
B. Tell her where the ship stands and what he doesn't know yet, in his own voice.
C. Skip the last log, and record a long, careful one to go out after the silence.
D. Keep the last log light and hopeful, and tell her the ship is on track.

He tells her plainly. The valve's root cause is still open, and the people on it are good, and he doesn't know what they'll find. The stage ships in July. The margin has two numbers and the board will pick one in July, and he believes hers. The team he runs is one team now, mostly. He doesn't tell her anything that's somebody else's to tell. Then he tells her he's scared of the silence, which he hadn't planned to, and that he'll record logs anyway and they'll all arrive at once, and she can skip the boring ones. He doesn't do the voice. He watches it back once and sends it at 1:52, and twenty one minutes and one second later it's on Mars.

Exactly right. Aligning expectations with a stakeholder means telling her what you know, what you don't, and what happens next, especially before a period when she can't ask. Honest uncertainty is a better last message than false confidence.

Thursday, May 25. 4:15 PM. Quinn had the elongation up on the big screen in the program room, refreshing every five minutes from the agency's feed, and people had drifted in from both buildings without anybody calling them. 3.0026. 3.0017. 3.0008. At 4:15 it said 2.9999, and the relay network's personal queue changed from OPEN to CLOSED in small gray letters, and nobody said anything. Wendell had come in from the stand for no reason he'd give. Copy, he said, to nobody.
His log had gone at 1:52. It was the first one in a long while that he hadn't watched back twice.
The beacon came through the next morning on its second try. It was one line, and it would be one line every sol for twenty two days.
Ares Station status beacon, sol 4005. Plant, green. Power, green. Life support, green. Medical, zero. The director's line: station nominal.

The program posted it unedited at 7:12, as he'd told the families it would, and every morning after that. Frances sent him a photograph of it on her refrigerator, held up by a magnet shaped like a little rocket.
Thursday, June 1. The cargo manifest closed at noon with six RP-55 bridge stacks on it, 430 kilograms with their mounts, and the station's sign off attached, dated May 19.
Saturday, June 3. Sol 4013. He read the beacon at 6:20 in the kitchen, standing up.
Ares Station status beacon, sol 4013. Plant, amber. Power, green. Life support, green. Medical, one. The director's line: station nominal.

The next sol the plant word was green again. One sol of amber wasn't a trigger, by the matrix he'd written himself, and he'd written it that way on purpose, and he read the line in the matrix again anyway. MED said 1 for seven sols. Two hundred and twelve people. It's always somebody's ankle. He didn't call anybody, because there was nobody to call who knew more than the beacon did. At nine Frances called him. I saw it. So did I. They stayed on the line for a while without saying much.

Monday, June 5. 10:00 PM. As close as it would get: from Earth, Mars was a little under half a degree from the middle of the Sun, a sliver of sky away from its edge. He sat at the kitchen table and recorded a log that wouldn't go anywhere for eleven days. He told her about Arlo's capitals on the high bay whiteboard, and the candles in the jars at the gate, and that he'd read the beacon every morning standing up. He didn't do the voice. There was nobody to do it for.

Monday, June 12. Twenty seven years since the Petrel. He recorded the second log at eight, with page nine on the table and the envelope still under his keys by the door, still addressed to Ruth, still not sealed. He didn't tell Ada whose page it was. He told her that a woman he knew had once told a commander yes when the true answer was I don't know, and that he was trying to learn to say the true one.

At the root cause meeting that afternoon the agency's reviewer sent Hana the first written comments. Your data are good. Your filing system is a crime. Hana read it out loud, and the room laughed, and Arlo laughed loudest.

Friday, June 16. 11:04 PM. The line passed. Nothing happened, because nothing could happen for at least twenty one minutes, and then the station would have to notice, and then the queue would have to drain. He was awake. He'd known he would be.
Saturday, June 17. 12:31 AM. The two note chime, for the first time in twenty two days. It wasn't a log.

ARES STATION MEDICAL CONJUNCTION SUMMARY SOL 4005 TO SOL 4027. ADMISSIONS: 1. OKAFOR, ADA. HYDROPONICS. ADMITTED SOL 4013. INJURIES SUSTAINED DURING OXYGEN PLANT REPAIR. DISCHARGED SOL 4020. FIT FOR LIGHT DUTY. CLINICAL DETAIL: RESTRICTED. RELEASE TO NEXT OF KIN ON REQUEST.
He read it three times. Under it, in the queue, there was nothing from her yet.

At 12:34 he sent the request as next of kin, one line, and sat at the kitchen table to wait for an answer that would take forty two and a half minutes at the very least, and probably until her morning. Twenty miles east, in an empty high bay, the countdown said 246.
